Chapter 2: The Weight of Judgment and the Policing of Bodies
Over the years, something strange happened. The body that once felt like a shield—something solid, something protective—suddenly became a target.
Have you ever noticed how the world seems to have endless opinions about fatness? Most of them are harsh, and plenty are hard to ignore. Just walking down the street, someone in a larger body can sense it all—the stares, the whispered insults, the heavy disapproval that seems to float in the air.
It’s almost like fatness makes you invisible and painfully visible, all at once.
And then there are public spaces. Airplane seats feel impossibly cramped, restaurant booths squeeze a little too tight, and finding clothes that actually fit? That’s a whole challenge on its own. Every one of these moments sends the same message: you don’t belong here.
Most people, moving through the world in bodies that fit the mold, never even notice these small humiliations. But for those living them, each one is like a tiny cut—a hurt that lingers, even if nobody else sees it.
Then there’s the doctor’s office. No matter why you’re there—maybe it’s just a sore throat or a twisted ankle—the conversation somehow always loops back to weight.
It’s as if every problem has the same supposed cause, and losing weight is the magic fix. There’s rarely room for nuance, for the truth that bodies are complicated and health isn’t just a numbers game.
For a lot of people, that judgment stings more than any illness, and they start avoiding medical care altogether.
And what about family gatherings? Well-meaning relatives pass along diet tips, glance at your plate, and bring up those “good old days” when you were thinner. The message is always the same: if only you were smaller, you’d be more lovable, more successful, somehow better.
It becomes clear that fatness isn’t just about size—it’s painted as a moral flaw, a sign you haven’t tried hard enough.
The media only makes things worse. On TV, in movies, in magazines, fat people are hardly ever the heroes—they’re the punchlines, the villains, or the warnings. Rarely do they get to be fully human, to fall in love, or to have a story that’s complex and real.
The world’s imagination is so limited, and anyone who lives outside those narrow boundaries ends up paying the price.
But then, in those quiet moments—away from the noise and the judgment—there’s space to think. And it becomes clear: the real problem isn’t the body itself, but the way the world treats it.
Fatness isn’t a crime, it isn’t a failure, and it’s not a reason to feel ashamed. It’s simply one way to be—a fact, not a flaw.
The real challenge? Holding on to that truth, even when the world keeps trying to take it away.
